newsitem.title: SPAIN: Jewish group calls on Spain in Nazi funds probe.
newsitem.headline: Jewish group calls on Spain in Nazi funds probe.

text.p: Leaders of a Jewish human rights group met Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Queen Sofia on Thursday to seek help in the international hunt for gold, art and other property stolen by Nazi Germany.

The U.S.-based Simon Wiesenthal Center asked Aznar to cooperate in a search of bank accounts which leading figures of the Third Reich may have used to hide funds in Spain and appealed to the government to reconsider the extradition of Nazis residing in Spain.

"The most important thing is that we gave Aznar a list of the 334 names and we asked him as we are going to ask all countries to participate with the Germans in a worldwide investigation into the perpetrators' accounts," Rabbi Marvin Hier, dean of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, told Reuters.
"Aznar replied that the government would be happy to investigate the names submitted and they would coordinate with the Germans," he added.
Until now the investigation on Nazi gold and assets has focused on two areas: the bank accounts of victims, and gold confiscated by conquering Nazis and placed with various central banks.
But the Jewish group said the real search should be for the Nazi elite's bank accounts as the assets of Holocaust victims were "peanuts" by comparison.

More than half a century after the war, an official investigation into the so-called perpetrator accounts has never been conducted. But three weeks ago, Germany announced it would start such an investigation, Hier said.
"When we find the funds we are going to say that they belong to the victims and if the governments or banks cashed the money, we're going to ask for it back," said Hier.
Individuals included in the list of 334 names range from Adolf Hitler to Nazi wives, mistresses, secretaries and agents.
On the extradition of Nazis living in Spain, the Center hopes the year-old conservative government will be more compliant than its Socialist predecessor.
"This is a new Spain that we are visiting here and I don't think the Spain of 1997 will put up with the arrogance of a Nazi looking for a safe haven," deputy dean Abraham Cooper said.
While Aznar's government has not yet responded to the extradition issue, the Justice Ministry is believed to be investigating certain cases.
"Spain is interested in clarifying everything," a government spokeswoman said.
After the Second World War, Spain harboured hundreds of Nazi war criminals under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.
Spain shifted from being officially neutral during the war to an ally of Adolf Hitler helping to fight against communism with its famed Blue Division volunteers.

Human rights organisations estimate just a handful of Nazi war criminals still remain in Spain, including former SS agent and Hitler's personal escort, Otto Remer who currently lives on the Costa del Sol.

"We are now dealing with a generation of leadership unencumbered by decisions in the Second World War and unencumbered even by the Cold War, and the younger generation want to give closure to survivors while they're still around," said Cooper.
